name: Omar Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a metal-bracket stamping press and measure the first piece after a die change. My vocational machine certificate and years on this shift make me an experienced mid-level operator, about average at the plant. A clean gauge fit is satisfying; a loose guard is not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Salma cooks at a school, our grown children have their own households, and we pay a mortgage. Night premiums lift my wage above the usual operator rate, we have eleven months saved, and plenty of similar plants are nearby. I have never used AI; I keep a paper setup list and ask a person about required forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little office software is the office’s affair. The stamping press still needs an operator who checks the die and measures the first bracket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a vocational certificate and know this press after years on it, but I am a regular experienced operator, not the tooling engineer. The night premium lifts my pay, my wife Salma cooks at a school, and our grown children earn their own living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the night shift, inspect the first bracket and use my paper checklist. We have eleven months of expenses saved and plenty of plants nearby; from each fresh full pay packet I would add a small amount to our separate retirement savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm in that world. I would rather spend breakfast with Salma than argue with a screen about a bracket I can measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first measurement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bracket hole has to line up with the gauge pin. A bad first piece means I stop the press before a whole bin is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. If the plant requires a new form, I want a person to show me during paid time, not an unpaid lesson at home.

Use **paper setup checklist** for every die change.
Save a **small amount** from each fresh full pay packet.
feel: **Calm** with present wages and substantial savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that scheduling software can help the office, but a robot loading a press must be guarded and tested. I want the paid rota in writing before anyone claims savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physical robot changes may take longer, and Salma’s school kitchen still needs hands. My own night shift could shrink if a loader replaces a second operator, though our savings and nearby plants give us room to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union representative to get a written shift plan and an offered paid demonstration on a locked-out press with the fitter present. I would watch the demonstration if offered, not operate a new control without taught practice; after an actual hours cut, I would apply for posted reachable press jobs only where pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible cut to my own hours, though not cornered. A guard on the press matters more to me than a promise about efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI controller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and watching a safe demonstration is not a licence to operate new controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose another plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the actual posting, weekly pay, travel time and night hours. Plenty of plants exist, but I need a real offer before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable press robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. Buying and scheduling may change first; the die and the loader change later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant could cut my night shift when robots can run the press. Eleven months saved and several nearby plants buy search time, but they do not promise that Salma’s wage alone would cover our mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a dated staffing and severance plan. If management gives a real cut notice, I would apply for posted reachable press or toolroom jobs only with bill-covering net pay after travel and a confirmed start date before resigning; I would postpone the new car while we compare wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my shift, but able to make calls before a bill goes unpaid. A full savings account is a clock, not another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual retirement income plus Salma’s confirmed wage covered housing, food and health costs. I have not priced that, so I would keep looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a rumour. There are nearby plants, and I would compare posted local terms first before changing home or job.

I would keep **press safety** on the union agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our apprentices that thinking AGI in 2031 comes when I am sixty-three, and capable press robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. Five years should buy safe training time for workers, not just a faster timetable for managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am slow with new screens but know how a stopped press fits together. A recognised tooling-maintenance certificate might let me keep earning if a nearby plant actually posts a job, though I will not give up a full wage for unpaid classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press shift and ask the union to bargain for a funded course on paid time. If an actual place is offered with supervised isolated-press practice and a posted reachable maintenance job with bill-covering pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role, or search posted press openings if no place appears and hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about later robot shifts but willing to learn with a fitter beside me. I would not put a hand under a die to earn a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the fitter show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would isolate the press, prove it dead and supervise a die alignment on a training block. I would not touch the live press for a class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used it and do not need to pretend otherwise. I would ask for taught mechanical work with paid hours and a real job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children that thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable press robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years gives Salma and me time to check the mortgage and real retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to finish full-time press work at sixty-seven, but eleven months saved is not a lifetime of bills. I have not seen what any pension pays, and I will not assume Salma’s school hours or our children’s wages carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the night press shift and add a little from each fresh full wage to retirement savings. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise I would continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and my hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while current wages and savings are solid. I want the final press shift to follow the arithmetic, not a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare real postings after travel if shifts fell. I would not assume a pension payment before seeing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I could ask for a lift to an appointment, but their income is not part of ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable press robots around 2031 could cut my night shift before we have settled the mortgage. Written staffing terms, offered funded paid safe training and posted work at bill-covering pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the guard is locked before the first bracket is stamped. I will put my name on a measured part, not on an unguarded shortcut.

headlineQuote: I will put my name on a measured part, not on an unguarded shortcut.
portrait: **Omar**, 58, is an experienced mid-level metal-stamping operator with vocational certification and average plant skill.
He has **higher night pay**, school-cook wife Salma, grown children, a mortgage, eleven months saved and plentiful nearby plants.
He **never uses AI**, favours union bargaining and would consider mechanical retraining only with offered funded paid safe practice.
Possible **2031 robot cuts** worry him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 press robots may cut night shifts before the mortgage is settled.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
